title: Dedicated capacity: Burst handoff & latency-aware prewarm PRD
creator: Ravi Patel
description: PRD for implementing a graceful burst handoff mechanism and latency-aware prewarming for Dedicated capacity pools. Goal is to allow tenants to safely exceed reserved throughput for short bursts while preserving latency SLOs for higher-priority tenants and minimizing evictions. Introduces a burst handoff policy, a background prewarm allocator, and observable signals to drive policy decisions.
problem_statement: Customers on Dedicated pools occasionally experience short traffic spikes that require more GPU slots than their reservation. Current behavior either rejects requests or preemptively evicts low-priority workload causing tail latency regressions and customer impact. We need a deterministic, observable, and tunable mechanism to handle bursts without impacting tenant SLAs.
goals: Allow controlled short-duration bursts up to configurable headroom per pool
Preserve P99/P95 latency SLOs for priority classes during burst events
Minimize noisy evictions and provide deterministic tenant-facing behavior
Provide observability and runbooks so SREs and account teams can explain incidents
Ship with rollout guardrails and opt-in controls for early customers
non_goals: Rearchitecting the entire scheduler — this is policy and feature work on top of existing scheduling stack
Realtime per-request price negotiation or per-token dynamic billing changes
Replacing existing RBAC and isolation guarantees for Private deployments
success_metrics: Reduction in eviction rate for low-priority tenants during burst windows by >= 60% vs baseline
Maintain P95 latency for high-priority tenancy classes within existing SLO (+/- 5%) across burst events
< 2% of bursts trigger manual intervention after rollout to opt-in customers
Telemetry surfaces: burst_count, average_burst_duration, prewarm_allocations, handoff_failures
user_stories: As an account owner, I can opt a tenant into burst handoff to allow short traffic spikes without manual capacity requests
As an SRE, I can see an event timeline showing prewarm allocations and handoff decisions during an incident
As a platform engineer, I can configure per-pool headroom, burst duration limits, and fairness weights
As a developer, my requests are not rejected during a short spike if headroom and prewarm are available
requirements: Policy: per-pool configurable headroom expressed in GPU slots or QPS equivalent
Policy: burst credit bucket per tenant that accrues at a rate and caps at a configured max
Prewarm allocator: background job that maintains a small warm pool of VMs/containers for each capacity class based on historical spike probability
Handoff: atomic path to transiently schedule a request on compatible pool when local reservation is saturated, subject to fairness weights
Eviction rules: ordered, deterministic eviction of low-priority scheduled work when handoff cannot be honored
Observability: dashboard tiles and traces for handoff events, prewarm fills, and eviction incidents
API/UI: controls in Console to opt-in tenants, configure headroom, and view burst credits
Backward compatibility: default behavior preserved (no burst) unless tenant opts in or pool admin enables
acceptance_criteria: E2E test: simulate 10k QPS spike for 120s — opt-in tenant that has 30% headroom should see <1% request errors and P95 latency within baseline +5%
Load test: under mixed-priority workload, eviction rate of non-critical tenants during bursts reduced by >=60% compared to baseline scheduler
Prewarm correctness: prewarm allocator must achieve >=80% successful cold-start avoidance for configured spike models in canary region
Observability: every handoff event emits a structured trace with tenant_id, pool_id, prewarm_used (true/false), start_ts, end_ts, and decision_reason
Console: Admin can set headroom per-pool and view current burst credits and active handoff events
Security: prewarm instances must inherit tenant isolation and network controls identical to normal instances (verified by security checklist)
implementation_notes: Leverage existing scheduler hooks in ENG-41207 to implement transient handoff path
Prewarm allocator implemented as separate service with a small state store; it should not be on critical path for request serving
Fairness weight calculation will reuse token from ENG-41788's weight engine with a per-burst multiplier
Telemetry will be stored in existing observability backend; add Grafana panels and a Console tile
Start with region-limited canary (us-west-2) and opt-in tenants only; gather 2 weeks of data before wider rollout
rollout_plan: Phase 0 (Design): Finalize policy primitives, acceptance tests, and SRE runbook — 2 weeks
Phase 1 (Canary): Implement feature behind feature flag; enable for 3 pilot customers in us-west-2 — 3 weeks
Phase 2 (Gradual rollout): Expand to all Dedicated pools with opt-in Console toggle; monitor metrics closely — 4 weeks
Phase 3 (Default enable for new pools): After 6 weeks of stable telemetry, enable for newly created pools by default; mature controls for existing customers via Admin opt-in — 6 weeks
Rollback: immediate toggle off of feature flag + eviction drain; documented runbook in Console incident page
monitoring_and_alerting: Alert if handoff_failures > 1% sustained for 5 minutes
Alert if prewarm_allocations unexpectedly exceed configured headroom for 3 consecutive windows
Runbook: if P95 latency for high-priority tenants degrades >10% during bursts, disable handoff globally and investigate traces
risks_and_mitigations: Risk: Prewarm cost overhead grows if misconfigured. Mitigation: conservative default prewarm size and cost-dashboard alerts
Risk: Complexity in scheduler could introduce regressions. Mitigation: comprehensive integration tests and staged rollout
Risk: Unexpected fairness inversion where low-priority tenants consume headroom. Mitigation: strict credit accounting and per-tenant caps
Risk: Customers misunderstand opt-in semantics. Mitigation: Console UX copy, in-app warnings, and account team outreach
open_questions: What is the canonical unit for headroom (GPU slots vs tokenized QPS) for cross-pool fairness? (decision needed from Runtime/Cost teams)
Should burst credits be transferable across pools owned by the same tenant? (cost and isolation implications)
What guardrails should apply to prewarm autoscaling to avoid global capacity churn?
How granular should per-tenant observability be to balance privacy and debuggability?
